title: Erste Schritte
welcome: This book is the paper half of A1.1. Every topic gets two facing pages: the **left page** teaches — tables, diagrams, the few rules that matter — and the **right page** is yours to write on.
Work with a pencil. Say every German word out loud as you write it; your mouth learns as much as your hand. When a page has a **Listen** code, scan it with your phone camera to hear the German.
The answers are at the back. Do a whole page first, then check, and circle what you got wrong — those circles are next week's revision.
At the foot of each practice page are three or four **I can** lines. Tick one only when you could do it tomorrow without the book.

spreads.title: Hallo! Das bin ich
spreads.subtitle: Greetings, introducing yourself, du and Sie
spreads.hook: Five questions, five answers — enough for your first conversation in German.

learn.title: Introduce yourself
learn.note: Ask a friend with *du*, a stranger with *Sie*. The answer is the same.

blocks.title: du or Sie?
blocks.note: Not sure? Say *Sie* — and wait for “Wir können du sagen”.

root.q: A friend, family, a child or another learner?

blocks.title: sie, sie or Sie?
blocks.text: *sie* is she, *sie* is they, and *Sie* with a capital S is the polite you. The verb gives it away: sie *ist* (she is), sie *sind* (they are), Sie *sind* (you are).

practise.title: du or Sie?
practise.instruction: Who gets *du*, who gets *Sie*? Write du or Sie.

practise.title: Question and answer
practise.instruction: Draw a line from each question to its answer.

practise.title: Max stellt sich vor
practise.instruction: Listen to Max introducing himself and complete the sentences.

practise.title: Now say it politely
practise.instruction: Rewrite each question with Sie.

practise.title: Das bin ich
practise.instruction: Write about yourself. Then say it out loud, without looking.
practise.note: About you — check each sentence against the table on the left page.

canDo: say hello and goodbye at any time of day
introduce myself in four sentences
ask the five questions with du and with Sie
choose between du and Sie

spreads.title: Zahlen 0–20
spreads.subtitle: Counting, and saying your phone number
spreads.hook: Twelve words to learn by heart. Every other German number is built from them.

learn.title: 0–12: learn these by heart
learn.note: Everything else is built from these.

blocks.title: Phone numbers
blocks.note: Digit by digit, or in pairs. On the phone, zwei is often *zwo*, so it can’t be heard as drei.

blocks.title: eins or ein?
blocks.text: Counting, the number on its own is *eins*: eins, zwei, drei. In front of a word it becomes *ein*: ein Euro, ein Kind. The der/die/das topic has the whole story.

blocks.title: Count from the thumb
blocks.text: The thumb is *eins*, thumb + index finger is *zwei*. Show three fingers the English way at a bakery and you may get two pretzels — or four.

practise.title: Write it in words
practise.instruction: Say each number out loud, then write it.

practise.title: Twins
practise.instruction: Each little number has a big twin. Draw a line from each number to its word.

practise.title: Phone numbers
practise.instruction: Read each number aloud digit by digit, then write it in words.

practise.title: Rechnen auf Deutsch
practise.instruction: Work it out and write the answer as a word.

practise.title: Your numbers
practise.instruction: Fill in your own numbers, in words. Then read the sentences aloud.
practise.note: Your own numbers — check the spelling against the left page.

canDo: count from 0 to 20 without stopping
spell sechzehn and siebzehn

spreads.title: Zahlen bis 100
spreads.subtitle: The tens, 21–99 and prices
spreads.hook: One pattern takes you to a hundred — then you can say every price in the shop.

learn.title: The tens: number + zig
learn.note: The same two trims as 16 and 17, and dreißig with ß.

learn.title: 21–99: say it backwards
learn.text: Small number first, then *und*, then the ten, all as one word, like the old English “four-and-twenty”. When you listen, wait for the end: the second half is the big part.

blocks.title: Prices
blocks.note: Euros, then cents. No word for the comma, and Euro never takes an -s.

blocks.title: Full stop and comma swap jobs
blocks.text: **1.200 €** is twelve hundred euros; **1,20 €** is one euro twenty. Read a German price tag the English way and you’ll be thrilled — for about a second.

practise.title: Write it in words
practise.instruction: Say each number out loud, then write it.

practise.title: Sixes and sevens
practise.instruction: These six are easy to mix up. Draw a line from each number to its word.

practise.title: Auf dem Markt
practise.instruction: Listen to the market seller and write each price on its tag. No phone? Ask someone to read you the prices from the answers.

practise.title: Prices
practise.instruction: Write each price the way you would say it.

practise.title: Your numbers
practise.instruction: Fill in your own numbers, in words. Then read the sentences aloud.
practise.note: Your own numbers — check the spelling against the left page.

canDo: say any number up to 100
hear the difference between 16 and 60
read a price like 3,49 € aloud
catch a price when someone says it

spreads.title: Das Alphabet
spreads.subtitle: Letters, spelling your name, A wie Anton
spreads.hook: Twenty-six letters you already know — six of them in disguise.

learn.title: Das Alphabet
learn.note: The six marked letters are the ones English speakers get wrong.

blocks.title: Six letters in disguise
blocks.text: **E** sounds like English A (*ay*), and **I** like English E (*ee*). **J** is *yot*, **V** is *fow*, **W** is *vay*, **Z** is *tset*. Spell VW out loud: *fow-vay*.

blocks.title: A wie Anton
blocks.text: On the phone, Germans spell with words: *A wie Anton*, *B wie Berta*, *M wie Martha*. Since 2022 the official list uses cities instead: *A wie Aachen*, *B wie Berlin*. Both are understood.

items.en: I’ll spell it: M – A – X.

learn.title: ä, ö, ü and ß
learn.text: The dots change the sound: *ä* is like the e in bed, *ö* is the ur in fur with round lips, *ü* is ee with round lips. *ß* is a double s after a long vowel: groß, heißen. Can’t write them? Use **ae, oe, ue, ss**: Muenchen, Tschuess.

practise.title: Letters in disguise
practise.instruction: Write the German name of each letter.

practise.title: Say it in letters
practise.instruction: Germans say these as letters. Write how they sound.

practise.title: Read the spelling
practise.instruction: Someone spells a word for you. Write the word.

items.prompt: Be – E – Er – El – I – En
Te – Es – Ce – Ha – U-Umlaut – Es – Es

practise.title: Dots or no dots?
practise.instruction: Write the missing letter: ä, ö, ü or ß.

practise.title: Your name, the German way
practise.instruction: Spell your first name in letters, then the phone way.
practise.note: About you — check each letter against the alphabet on the left page.

practise.title: Say it in German
practise.instruction: Write it in German.

canDo: say the alphabet
spell my name

spreads.title: sein & haben
spreads.subtitle: I am, I have — the two verbs you use most
spreads.hook: You can’t say much without these two. Both are irregular, so they go in by heart.

learn.title: sein and haben
learn.note: sein has no pattern at all. haben is regular, except that du *hast* and er *hat* lose the b.

blocks.title: Hungry? Use haben
blocks.text: German *has* hunger: Ich habe **Hunger** (I’m hungry), **Durst** (thirsty), **Angst** (afraid), **Zeit** (I have time). But your age is sein: Ich *bin* zwanzig.

blocks.title: wir and sie are twins
blocks.text: In both verbs, *wir* and *sie · Sie* have the same form: wir sind, sie sind; wir haben, sie haben. Learn four forms, get six.

practise.instruction: Write the right form of sein.

practise.title: haben
practise.instruction: Write the right form of haben.

practise.title: sein or haben?
practise.instruction: Circle the right word.

practise.title: And you, today?
practise.instruction: Write two true sentences about yourself.
practise.note: About you — check it against the left page.

canDo: say all six forms of sein
say all six forms of haben
say I’m hungry, thirsty or tired
choose between sein and haben

spreads.title: Verben im Präsens
spreads.subtitle: What you do every day: regular verbs
spreads.hook: Cut off the -en, add the ending. Six endings, and they fit every regular verb.

learn.title: Stem + ending
learn.note: wohnen → wohn- → wohn*e*. wir and sie always look like the infinitive.

blocks.title: Stem + ending
blocks.note: After -t or -d an e slips in.

blocks.title: One present, three Englishes
blocks.text: *Ich wohne in Berlin* is I live, I’m living and I do live in Berlin. Never try to build “I am living” in German.

items.en: gladly — Ich spiele gern = I like playing

learn.note: a → ä · e → i · e → ie

spreads.title: der, die, das
spreads.subtitle: Every noun has one — learn it with the word
spreads.hook: Not “Tisch = table” but “der Tisch = table”. The article is part of the word.

learn.title: Three articles
learn.note: ein for der and das, eine for die.

blocks.title: Three pencils
blocks.text: Write every new der-word in blue, die in red and das in green. After a week, your hand knows the colour before your head does.

blocks.title: das Mädchen
blocks.text: A girl is *das* Mädchen: every word ending in -chen is das, whatever it means. Gender is grammar, not biology.

spreads.title: Plural
spreads.subtitle: One table, two tables: five ways to say more
spreads.hook: English adds -s. German has five endings — and one article for all of them: die.

learn.title: Five endings
rows: die Lampe · die Katze · die Frau
die Lampe*n* · die Katze*n* · die Frau*en*
das Haus · das Buch · das Kind
die H*ä*us*er* · die B*ü*ch*er* · die Kind*er*
learn.note: ¨ means: add the dots. – means: no ending.

blocks.title: Always die
blocks.text: Every plural takes *die*, whatever the word was before: der Tisch → *die* Tische, das Kind → *die* Kinder.

blocks.title: How word lists write it
blocks.text: **der Tisch, -e** · **das Haus, ¨-er** · **der Schlüssel, -**. The bit after the comma is the plural. Learn it with the word, like the article.
